items.notes: Real headless-browser capture, 1280x900 @2x. The sentence was typed into the System box by the research agent (it replaced the default text); the dek is that typed input, not a page quote. Page shows no publication date, so date is the capture date. Token IDs in the panel: 200264, 17360, 200266 (chat header) then 30325, 553, 3291, 12762, 328, 2201, 13, 50258, 1729, 1373, 1001, 540, 261, 1058, 13 (the 15 sentence tokens) then 200265, 200264, 1428, 200266, 200265, 200264, 173781, 200266 (chat footer). items.slide_topic: Next-token prediction: the one training objective behind LLMs
items.headline: LLM Fundamentals
items.dek: A large language model is a neural network trained on massive amounts of text data to predict the next token in a sequence.
items.caption: Microsoft Learn 'LLM Fundamentals' one-line definition of next-token prediction.
items.notes: Page title 'LLM Fundamentals | Microsoft Learn'. Same page also says: 'Pretraining is where the model learns the bulk of its knowledge. The model is fed massive amounts of text from the internet ... and learns to predict the next token given all previous tokens.' Generation loop on the same page: the model 'produces a probability distribution over its vocabulary', the chosen token 'is appended to the full sequence', and the sequence is fed back in.

items.slide_topic: Next-token prediction: pretraining first, then fine-tuning
items.headline: Large language model
items.dek: Before being fine-tuned, most LLMs are next-token predictors.
items.caption: Wikipedia 'Large language model' article: most LLMs are next-token predictors before fine-tuning (RLHF and constitutional AI are named as fine-tuning methods).
items.notes: Wording from the loaded page; the article's citation marker [28] removed. Same article, same section: 'GPT models are first pretrained to predict the next word on a large amount of data, before being fine-tuned.' Page version is the one loaded on 2026-10-10 (no publication date on Wikipedia).

facts.claim: Tokens are the units that OpenAI models use to process text. A token can represent a character, part of a word, a whole word, or punctuation.
facts.source: OpenAI Help Center, 'Understanding and counting tokens' (Overview section)
OpenAI Help Center, 'Understanding and counting tokens' (section 'Use rough estimates for English text'). Same section: 'These are estimates, not exact counts.'

facts.claim: 1 token is approximately three-quarters of a word. 100 tokens are approximately 75 words.
facts.source: OpenAI Help Center, 'Understanding and counting tokens' (section 'Use rough estimates for English text'). OpenAI calls these estimates, not exact counts, and notes other languages differ.

facts.claim: Derived: an English word is about 1.33 tokens on average (1 divided by 0.75), so about 4 tokens per 3 words.
facts.source: Arithmetic on the OpenAI Help Center ratio ('1 token is approximately three-quarters of a word'). Derived by the research agent, not stated by OpenAI.

facts.claim: A token count is not the same as a word count. The same text can produce different token counts depending on the model, its encoding, and the language.
facts.source: OpenAI Help Center, 'Understanding and counting tokens' (Overview section)

facts.claim: The sentence 'Tokens are small pieces of text. Models read them one at a time.' (13 words) is 15 tokens in the gpt-4o tokenizer on Tiktokenizer, about 1.15 tokens per word for this one sentence.
facts.source: Measured by the research agent on Tiktokenizer (gpt-4o) on 2026-10-10. Third-party tool, not an OpenAI statement. The page's total of 26 includes 11 chat-format tokens.
